newsitem.title: UK: Copper falls on LME, ends below $2,200.
newsitem.headline: Copper falls on LME, ends below $2,200.

text.p: Copper turned lower with a vengeance during Monday LME kerb trading with a downturn below $2,200 triggering sell-stops and fresh selling, and prices ended at the day's lows.

Traders said narrowing spread backwardations, a perception that there would be another small inventory increase on Tuesday, and less concern over high upside call options being declared on Wednesday sent a volatile market lower. But conditions are seen remaining volatile, and prices may easily whip higher again.
"It would not take much to get it (the market) up, and it is still short going in to the options," one said.

The market weakened from the outset of afternoon trading, with losses in New York in post-Thanksgiving holiday trading augmenting the trend, and with spread premiums softening stops were eventually hit on both sides of the Atlantic.
Last kerb business was at $2,187 a tonne, down $55 from Friday's kerb close, and compared with last week's six-month peak of $2,313.
Cash/threes narrowed as well, and was around $185 at the close, against $245 on Friday and the high-point last week of $285.

Stocks on Tuesday are expected to register an increase of some 2,000 to 4,000 tonnes. But even though inventories will have risen for two successive reports if the forecasts prove accurate, the market remains critically short of metal.
Copper's late losses knocked the stuffing out of the rest of the metals complex, and nearly all other markets turned lower to end in the minus column.
Aluminium finished at $1,518, down $11 from Friday, but is still looking to consolidate after last week's advances to six-month highs. Stocks are seen lower tomorrow.
Lead was boosted by news of output losses at Doe Run's Buick secondary facility, caused by furnace problems. Prices peaked abvove $690 before settling back with copper to end at $688, still up $2.
Zinc paid little heed to news that Noranda's Heath Steele mine in New Brunswick has been closed since an accident on Friday. The market sagged in late trade and closed at $1,066, down $5.
Tin was supported around the $6,100 level, which helped to restrict losses, and last business was at $6,100, down just $10.
Nickel was partially helped by short-covering, and closed at $6,840, up $20.
Alloy was slow, but held fairly steady to close at $1,358/60 a tonne.
